html:
A huge volcanic eruption on the Aegean island of Thera, now Santorini, around 1600 BCE, one of the largest in human history. The middle of the island collapsed into the sea, leaving the ring-shaped bay seen today.

It buried the Bronze Age town of Akrotiri under metres of ash. The people seem to have left in time, since few bodies have been found. The houses, two and three storeys high, kept their wall paintings of boats, monkeys, lilies and boxing boys, so Akrotiri is sometimes called the Bronze Age Pompeii.

Ash fell over Crete and Anatolia, and tsunamis struck nearby coasts. Minoan Crete survived, but declined over the next century or two, and Mycenaean Greeks took over Knossos. The exact date is disputed: radiocarbon points to the late 1600s BCE, while links with Egyptian history suggest a century later. Some connect the disaster with the legend of Atlantis told by Plato.
sum: A huge volcanic eruption on the Aegean island of Thera, now Santorini, around 1600 BCE, one of the largest in human history. The middle of the island collapsed into the sea, leaving the ring-shaped bay seen today.
